public_rationale: Obscurity Labs' April 29–May 10, 2024 inspection found that Rabbit collected service-issued session cookies for storage, rather than the usernames and passwords entered during login [e1](https://www.obscuritylabs.com/resources/blog/rabbit_pentest). This contradicts the asserted need to retain original app passwords for subsequent operations [e1](https://www.obscuritylabs.com/resources/blog/rabbit_pentest).
limitations: The inspection covers part of the April 23–May 13 target period; the report became available on July 30, 2024.
The commissioned assessment excluded testing of the secrets vault itself and does not establish that Rabbit's entire system was secure.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Rabbit must store user credentials in original form, which is insanely dangerous.

statement.excerpt: Since Rabbit is acting as a third-party, and doesn’t use a standard like Oauth or SAML, it needs to keep user credentials in their original form. This is just insanely dangerous.

from_speaker: doesn’t use a standard like Oauth or SAML

our_interpretation: In the surrounding discussion of password hashing, original credentials means recoverable usernames and passwords, including reversibly encrypted passwords. It does not mean session cookies.
Assess the technical assertion about retention. The phrase insanely dangerous is an evaluative description without a separate measurable threshold.
Use the launch-period implementation from April 23 through May 13, the latest public operating period described by the post.
criteria.support_condition: Implementation evidence shows that Rabbit retained recoverable original app passwords for subsequent operations.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Implementation evidence shows that Rabbit retained session cookies or tokens instead of original app passwords, allowing subsequent operations without keeping those passwords.
